claim: Mammalian cells express up to three nonmuscle myosin II isoforms termed NM IIA, B, and C.
source: Mammalian cells express up to three isoforms termed NM IIA, B, and C.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by established scientific knowledge about myosin II isoforms.

claim: U2OS cells were used to create CRISPR/Cas9-based knockouts of all three NM II isoforms.
source: We used U2OS cells to create CRISPR/Cas9-based knockouts of all three isoforms and analyzed the phenotypes on homogenously coated surfaces, in collagen gels, and on micropatterned substrates.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: A structured environment supports a cellular phenotype with invaginated actin arcs even in the absence of NM IIA-induced contractility.
source: In contrast to homogenously coated surfaces, a structured environment supports a cellular phenotype with invaginated actin arcs even in the absence of NM IIA-induced contractility.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data on micropatterned substrates.

claim: NM IIA is essential to build up cellular tension during initial stages of force generation.
source: A quantitative shape analysis of cells on micropatterns combined with a scale-bridging mathematical model reveals that NM IIA is essential to build up cellular tension during initial stages of force generation, while NM IIB is necessary to elastically stabilize NM IIA-generated tension.
evidence: This conclusion is derived from quantitative analysis combined with mathematical modeling of experimental data.

claim: NM IIB is necessary to elastically stabilize NM IIA-generated tension.
source: A quantitative shape analysis of cells on micropatterns combined with a scale-bridging mathematical model reveals that NM IIA is essential to build up cellular tension during initial stages of force generation, while NM IIB is necessary to elastically stabilize NM IIA-generated tension.
evidence: This conclusion is derived from quantitative analysis combined with mathematical modeling of experimental data.

claim: NM IIC has the ability to establish tensional homeostasis.
source: A dynamic cell stretch/release experiment in a three-dimensional scaffold confirms these conclusions and in addition reveals a novel role for NM IIC, namely the ability to establish tensional homeostasis.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the 3D stretching experiments presented in the study.

claim: NM II hexamers assemble into bipolar filaments of up to 30 hexamers with a typical size of 300 nm.
source: Individual NM II hexamers assemble into bipolar filaments of up to 30 hexamers with a typical size of 300 nm, termed myosin minifilaments.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about myosin II organization.

claim: NM II minifilaments can generate tension between antiparallel actin filaments due to their ATP-dependent motor activity.
source: These minifilaments can generate tension between antiparallel actin filaments due to their ATP-dependent motor activity.
evidence: This describes the fundamental mechanism of myosin II function, which is established knowledge.

claim: NM II generated forces are transmitted throughout the cell by subcellular structures such as the actomyosin cortex and different stress fiber subtypes.
source: NM II generated forces are transmitted throughout the cell by subcellular structures such as the actomyosin cortex and different stress fiber subtypes (SFs) (Burnette et al., 2014; Hotulainen and Lappalainen, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Stress fibers are anchored to the extracellular matrix via integrin-based focal adhesions.
source: Since SFs are anchored to the extracellular matrix (ECM) via integrin-based focal adhesions (FAs), adherent cells are able to sense the physical properties of their environment at the cell-substrate interface (Geiger et al., 2009), where high forces can be measured with traction force microscopy (Balaban et al., 2001; Oakes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established research on focal adhesions and force sensing.

claim: All NM II hexamer isoforms contain the same set of light chains but vary with respect to their heavy chains.
source: All hexamer-isoforms, which are commonly termed NM IIA, NM IIB, and NM IIC, contain the same set of light chains but vary with respect to their heavy chains, which are encoded by three different genes (Heissler and Manstein, 2013).
evidence: This structural information is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The loss of NM IIA and NM IIB causes severe phenotypes in the corresponding KO-mice.
source: While the cell type-dependent expression, structure, and function of NM IIC is still not clear, the loss of NM IIA and NM IIB causes severe phenotypes in the corresponding KO-mice (Conti et al., 2004; Ma et al., 2010; Takeda et al., 2003; Tullio et al., 1997; Tullio et al., 2001; Uren et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous mouse knockout studies.

claim: The loss of NM IIA drastically impairs SF formation, FA elongation, and cellular force generation.
source: On the cellular level, the loss of NM IIA drastically impairs SF formation, FA elongation, and cellular force generation, while the loss of NM IIB only causes mild deficiencies during SF and FA consolidation, cell shape stabilization, and force generation (Barua et al., 2014; Beach et al., 2017; Betapudi et al., 2006; Billington et al., 2013; Even-Ram et al., 2007; Jorrisch et al., 2013; Sandquist and Means, 2008; Sandquist et al., 2006; Shutova et al., 2012; Shutova et al., 2017; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2008; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2011; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to previous cellular studies.

claim: The loss of NM IIB only causes mild deficiencies during SF and FA consolidation, cell shape stabilization, and force generation.
source: On the cellular level, the loss of NM IIA drastically impairs SF formation, FA elongation, and cellular force generation, while the loss of NM IIB only causes mild deficiencies during SF and FA consolidation, cell shape stabilization, and force generation (Barua et al., 2014; Beach et al., 2017; Betapudi et al., 2006; Billington et al., 2013; Even-Ram et al., 2007; Jorrisch et al., 2013; Sandquist and Means, 2008; Sandquist et al., 2006; Shutova et al., 2012; Shutova et al., 2017; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2008; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2011; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to previous cellular studies.

claim: NM IIA propels actin filaments 3.5× faster than NM IIB.
source: NM IIA propels actin filaments 3.5× faster than NM IIB and generates fast contractions (Kovács et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This quantitative difference is supported by citations to biochemical studies.

claim: NM IIB can bear more load due to its higher duty ratio.
source: NM IIB can bear more load due to its higher duty ratio (Pato et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: This biochemical property is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: NM IIA and NM IIB hexamers co-assemble into heterotypic minifilaments.
source: Cell culture studies furthermore revealed that NM IIA and NM IIB hexamers co-assemble into heterotypic minifilaments, with a NM IIA to NM IIB gradient from the front to the rear of the cell (Beach et al., 2014; Shutova et al., 2014).
evidence: This organizational feature is supported by citations to cell culture studies.

claim: There is a NM IIA to NM IIB gradient from the front to the rear of the cell.
source: Cell culture studies furthermore revealed that NM IIA and NM IIB hexamers co-assemble into heterotypic minifilaments, with a NM IIA to NM IIB gradient from the front to the rear of the cell (Beach et al., 2014; Shutova et al., 2014).
evidence: This spatial distribution is supported by citations to cell culture studies.

claim: The composition of heterotypic minifilaments tunes contractility during cell polarization and migration.
source: Recent publications provide detailed insights that the composition of these heterotypic minifilaments tune contractility during cell polarization and migration (Shutova et al., 2017) or cytokinesis (Taneja et al., 2020).
evidence: This functional role is supported by citations to recent publications.

claim: U2OS is a model system for the investigation of stress fibers.
source: Using CRISPR/Cas9 technology, we generated isoform-specific NM II-KO cells from the U2OS cell line, which is a model system for the investigation of SFs (Hotulainen and Lappalainen, 2006; Jiu et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2018; Tojkander et al., 2015; Tojkander et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations establishing U2OS as a model system.

claim: Polarized U2OS WT cells form numerous stress fibers of different subtypes.
source: Polarized U2OS WT cells form numerous SFs of different subtypes, as previously described (Hotulainen and Lappalainen, 2006; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1A showing the phenotype.

claim: Depletion of NM IIA leads to a markedly altered cellular phenotype with a branched morphology and several lamellipodia.
source: Depletion of NM IIA leads to a markedly altered cellular phenotype with a branched morphology and several lamellipodia (Figure 1B; Doyle et al., 2012; Even-Ram et al., 2007; Sandquist et al., 2006; Shih and Yamada, 2010; Shutova et al., 2017).
evidence: This phenotype is shown in Figure 1B and supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: No ordered SF-network is built up in NM IIA-KO cells and only few ventral SFs remain.
source: No ordered SF-network is built up and only few ventral SFs remain.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data on NM IIA-KO cells.

claim: Mature, elongated FAs are absent in NM IIA-KO cells.
source: Mature, elongated FAs are absent in NM IIA-KO cells (Figure 1E&F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The effect of the NM IIB-KO is less severe and does not affect overall cell morphology.
source: The effect of the NM IIB-KO is less severe and does not affect overall cell morphology (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation supported by Figure 1C.

claim: All subtypes of SFs are present in NM IIB-KO cells, but their distinct cellular localization is missing in many cells.
source: All subtypes of SFs are present, but their distinct cellular localization is missing in many cells.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data on NM IIB-KO cells.

claim: Numerous mature FAs were observed throughout the cell body in NM IIB-KO cells but their frequency was lower compared to WT cells.
source: Numerous mature FAs were observed throughout the cell body but their frequency was lower compared to WT cells (Figure 1E and F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The depletion of NM IIC did not reveal any phenotypic differences compared to WT cells.
source: The depletion of NM IIC did not reveal any phenotypic differences compared to WT cells (Figure 1D–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The cell area does not significantly differ between WT and NM II-KO cells.
source: In addition, the cell area does not significantly differ between WT and NM II-KO cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The ratio of NM IIA to NM IIB minifilaments in WT cells is roughly 4.5:1.
source: Measuring GFP signals along segmented actin fibers revealed that the ratio of NM IIA to NM IIB is roughly 4.5:1 (Figure 2A&B).
evidence: This quantitative measurement is shown in Figure 2A&B using fluorescent knock-in cells.

claim: Overexpression of NM IIB in NM IIA-KO cells does not restore the WT phenotype.
source: However, the distribution of NM IIB was still strongly clustered along single SF and does not compare to the distribution of NM IIA in WT cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and related panels.

claim: Even strongest overexpression of NM IIB could not phenocopy the pRLC level of WT cells.
source: While the pRLC intensity was drastically reduced in NM IIA-KO cells, even strongest overexpression of NM IIB could not phenocopy the pRLC level of WT cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown by quantitative data in Figure 2C measuring phosphorylated RLC as a marker for active myosin.

claim: No difference in surface tension was observed for NM IIC-KO cells compared to WT.
source: No difference was observed for NM IIC-KO cells.
evidence: This is stated in the context of AFM nanoindentation measurements.

claim: Not only the absolute quantity of NM II molecules but rather the qualitative properties of both NM IIA and B are necessary for the formation of a fully functional actomyosin cytoskeleton.
source: Thus, not only the absolute quantity of NM II molecules but rather the qualitative properties of both, NM IIA and B, are necessary for the formation of a fully functional actomyosin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the overexpression experiments and other data showing that quantity alone cannot compensate for loss of specific isoforms.

claim: Gel contraction was highest in WT and NM IIC-KO gels in cell-seeded collagen gels.
source: We found that the gel contraction was highest in WT and NM IIC-KO gels, followed by slightly reduced values when using NM IIB-KO cells, and almost no contraction for NM IIA-KO cells.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the collagen gel contraction experiments.

claim: NM IIA-KO cells show almost no contraction in cell-seeded collagen gels.
source: We found that the gel contraction was highest in WT and NM IIC-KO gels, followed by slightly reduced values when using NM IIB-KO cells, and almost no contraction for NM IIA-KO cells.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the collagen gel contraction experiments.

claim: All cell lines flattened in the collagen gel and showed phenotypes with concave, inward bent actin arcs that line the cell contour.
source: All cell lines flattened in the collagen gel and in contrast to the cell morphologies on FN-coated coverslips, we now observed phenotypes with concave, inward bent actin arcs that line the cell contour as previously described for various cell types (Bischofs et al., 2008; Brand et al., 2017; Kassianidou et al., 2019; Labouesse et al., 2015; Tabdanov et al., 2018; Théry et al., 2006).
evidence: This observation is supported by citations to previous studies showing similar phenotypes.

claim: WT and all NM II-KO cell lines reveal a similar phenotype on micropatterned substrates with actin arcs bridging the passivated substrate areas.
source: Like in collagen gels, all cell lines adapted their shape to the pattern and gained a striking phenotype with concave, inward bent actin arcs that line the cell contour (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 for all cell lines on micropatterned substrates.

claim: NM II minifilaments localize along the circular actin arcs on micropatterned substrates.
source: NM II minifilaments localize along the circular actin arcs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–D), indicating that they are contractile SFs.
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence imaging in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: The circularity of actin arcs results from two different NM II-based contributions to cell mechanics: tension in the cortex (surface tension σ) and tension in the actin arcs (line tension λ).
source: From a geometrical point of view, the circularity results from two different NM II-based contributions to cell mechanics: tension in the cortex (surface tension σ) and tension in the actin arcs (line tension λ).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation based on mechanical principles.

claim: Balancing surface tension and line tension can explain circular actin arcs with the radius R = λ/σ (Laplace law).
source: Balancing these tensions can explain circular actin arcs with the radius R = λ/σ (Laplace law).
evidence: This applies the Laplace law to explain the observed circular arc geometry.

claim: WT cells regularly form actin arcs along all cell edges on micropatterned substrates.
source: WT cells regularly form actin arcs along all cell edges (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: WT cells show a positive correlation (r = 0.63 ± 0.06) between arc radius R and spanning distance d.
source: Quantitative evaluation showed a positive correlation (r = 0.63 ± 0.06) of R with increasing d, as observed previously (Bischofs et al., 2008; Brand et al., 2017; Tabdanov et al., 2018).
evidence: This quantitative correlation is measured from the experimental data and consistent with previous studies.

claim: NM IIA-KO cells formed circular arcs and obeyed a clear R(d)-correlation (r = 0.61 ± 0.06) on micropatterned substrates.
source: Surprisingly, NM IIA-KO cells formed circular arcs and also obeyed a clear R(d)-correlation (r = 0.61 ± 0.06) (Figure 3B), despite the fact that their phenotype was strongly affected on homogenously coated FN-substrates.
evidence: This surprising finding is quantified from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The structured environment can support an invaginated phenotype even in the absence of NM IIA-induced contractility.
source: This agrees with our observations in the collagen gels and shows that the structured environment can support an invaginated phenotype even in the absence of NM IIA-induced contractility.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that NM IIA-KO cells form arcs on structured substrates.

claim: NM IIA-KO cells have fewer internal SFs compared to WT cells as shown by weaker image coherency.
source: Compared to WT cells, fewer internal SFs are present as shown by a weaker image coherency (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is quantified using image analysis shown in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: The pRLC staining is almost completely absent in NM IIA-KO cells on micropatterned substrates, suggesting that contractile forces are low.
source: NM IIB minifilaments co-localize along the actin arcs in NM IIA-KO cells and the pRLC staining is almost completely absent, suggesting that contractile forces are low in these cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence imaging in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: In NM IIB-KO cells, the R(d)-correlation was strongly reduced (r = 0.33 ± 0.09) on micropatterned substrates.
source: Surprisingly, in NM IIB-KO cells the R(d)-correlation was strongly reduced (r = 0.33 ± 0.09) (Figure 3C), caused by the presence of a mixed population of bent and almost straight arcs that develop independent of the spanning distance d.
evidence: This quantitative finding is measured from the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: NM IIB-KO cells have a mixed population of bent and almost straight arcs that develop independent of the spanning distance d.
source: Surprisingly, in NM IIB-KO cells the R(d)-correlation was strongly reduced (r = 0.33 ± 0.09) (Figure 3C), caused by the presence of a mixed population of bent and almost straight arcs that develop independent of the spanning distance d.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: NM IIC-KO cells did not reveal any differences concerning their morphology and the R(d)-correlation was comparable to WT cells (r = 0.63 ± 0.06) on micropatterned substrates.
source: NM IIC-KO cells did not reveal any differences concerning their morphology and the R(d)-correlation was comparable to WT cells (r = 0.63 ± 0.06) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is measured from the experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Overexpressing GFP-NM IIB in NM IIA-KO cells did not restore the WT phenotype on micropatterned substrates.
source: Importantly, overexpressing GFP-NM IIB in NM IIA-KO cells did not restore the WT phenotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is shown in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: Overexpressing GFP-NM IIA in NM IIB-KO cells did not significantly increase the R(d)-correlation.
source: Similarly, overexpressing GFP-NM IIA in NM IIB-KO cells did not significantly increase the R(d)-correlation (r = 0.49 ± 0.07) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is shown in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: NM IIA-KO cells form actin arcs with small arc radii that are correlated to the spanning distance.
source: These results reveal opposing functions for NM IIA and NM IIB in cell shape determination on structured substrates. NM IIA-KO cells form actin arcs with small arc radii that are correlated to the spanning distance, while NM IIB-KO cells form actin arcs with large arc radii that are not correlated to the spanning distance.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental observations on micropatterned substrates.

claim: NM IIB-KO cells form actin arcs with large arc radii that are not correlated to the spanning distance.
source: These results reveal opposing functions for NM IIA and NM IIB in cell shape determination on structured substrates. NM IIA-KO cells form actin arcs with small arc radii that are correlated to the spanning distance, while NM IIB-KO cells form actin arcs with large arc radii that are not correlated to the spanning distance.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental observations on micropatterned substrates.

claim: The main difference in the crossbridge cycles is that NM IIA generates faster contractions and NM IIB bears more load.
source: The main difference in the crossbridge cycles are that NM IIA generates faster contractions (Wang et al., 2000; Kovács et al., 2003) and NM IIB bears more load (Wang et al., 2003; Pato et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to biochemical studies of the motor properties.

claim: With increasing NM IIB content in minifilaments, the stall force increases and the free velocity decreases.
source: With increasing NM IIB content, the stall force increases and the free velocity decreases, which is mainly an effect of the much smaller duty ratio of NM IIA (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is calculated from the mathematical model and shown in the referenced appendix figure.

claim: NM IIB stabilizes tension due to its slower crossbridge cycle.
source: This agrees with our theoretical finding that NM IIB stabilizes tension due to its slower crossbridge cycle (Grewe and Schwarz, 2020a; Grewe and Schwarz, 2020b).
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the theoretical model and citations to related work.

claim: U2OS WT cells generated a mean initial force of 94 nN in 3D micro-scaffolds.
source: U2OS WT cells generated a mean initial force of 94 nN (Figure 5B and Figure 5—animation 1), while NM IIA-KO cells generated almost no traction forces (Figure 5—animation 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) with a mean value of 11 nN (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is measured from the 3D scaffold experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: NM IIA-KO cells generated almost no traction forces with a mean value of 11 nN in 3D micro-scaffolds.
source: U2OS WT cells generated a mean initial force of 94 nN (Figure 5B and Figure 5—animation 1), while NM IIA-KO cells generated almost no traction forces (Figure 5—animation 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) with a mean value of 11 nN (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is measured from the 3D scaffold experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: NM IIB-KO cells generated a mean initial force of 112 nN in 3D micro-scaffolds, which did not significantly differ from WT cells.
source: When measuring the initial forces of NM IIB-KO cells, we obtained a mean value of 112 nN (Figure 5B, Figure 5—animation 3 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), which did not significantly differ from WT cells.
evidence: This is measured from the 3D scaffold experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: NM IIC-KO cells showed no significant difference to the WT in initial forces with a mean force value of 110 nN.
source: NM IIC-KO cells also showed no significant difference to the WT (Figure 5—animation 4 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) with a mean force value of 110 nN (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is measured from the 3D scaffold experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: WT cells actively counteract the stretch and increase their contractile forces until reaching a plateau after approximately 30-40 min.
source: As previously described (Hippler et al., 2020), WT U2OS cells show a typical response to this stretch-release cycle: Cells counteract the stretch by increasing their traction forces over a time course of ~ 30 min until they settle on a new plateau value (Figure 5—animation 5 and Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in the stretch-release experiments in Figure 5D and referenced animation.

claim: After releasing the stretch, WT cells decrease their traction forces again and settle at the initial force value.
source: After releasing the stretch, WT cells decrease their traction forces again and settle at the initial force value.
evidence: This is observed in the stretch-release experiments.

claim: NM IIA-KO cells show no reaction to the stretch-release cycle, even after increasing the stretch period to 70 min.
source: When applying the stretch-release cycle to NM IIA-KO cells, the cells show no reaction, even after increasing the stretch period to 70 min (Hippler et al., 2020; Figure 5E and Figure 5—animation 6).
evidence: This is shown in the stretch-release experiments in Figure 5E and supported by a citation.

claim: NM IIB-KO cells revealed a clear response to the stretch-release cycle similar to WT cells.
source: In contrast, NM IIB-KO cells revealed a clear response to the stretch-release cycle similar to WT cells (Figure 5F and Figure 5—animation 7).
evidence: This is shown in the stretch-release experiments in Figure 5F.

claim: 80% of the NM IIC-KO cells did not decrease their intracellular forces after release within the monitored timeframe of 30 min.
source: However, 80% of the NM IIC-KO cells did not decrease their intracellular forces after release within the monitored timeframe of 30 min (Figure 5G and H, Figure 5—animation 8 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is quantified from the stretch-release experiments shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: WT cells showed a mean force increase of 72 nN upon stretching.
source: Quantifying the force increase (within the blue boxes in Figure 5D–G) showed a mean value of 72 nN for WT cells and no mean force increase for NM IIA-KO cells (Hippler et al., 2020).
evidence: This is quantified from the stretch experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: NM IIB-KO cells revealed a force increase of 41 nN upon stretching, which was significantly lower than in WT cells.
source: NM IIB-KO cells also revealed a force increase of 41 nN which was, however, significantly lower than in WT cells (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is quantified from the stretch experiments shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The force increase of NM IIC-KO cells did not significantly differ from WT cells, but the mean variation was higher.
source: The force increase of NM IIC-KO cells did not significantly differ from WT cells, but the mean variation was higher.
evidence: This is observed from the quantification of the stretch experiments.

claim: NM IIA initiates cellular tension, while NM IIB contributes to this tension by providing elastic stability for a stable force output on longer time-scales.
source: These data strongly support our hypothesis that NM IIA initiates cellular tension, while NM IIB contributes to this tension by providing elastic stability for a stable force output on longer time-scales, that is during the mechanoresponse of cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the stretch-release experiments and modeling.

claim: NM IIC plays a role in the temporal control of the force relaxation, that is the mechanical homeostasis of cells.
source: In addition, NM IIC seems to play a role in the temporal control of the force relaxation, that is the mechanical homeostasis of cells.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that NM IIC-KO cells fail to relax forces after stretch release.

claim: The marked phenotypic differences of NM IIA-KO cells are dampened when the cells were cultivated in a structured environment.
source: To our surprise, the marked phenotypic differences of NM IIA-KO cells are dampened when the cells were cultivated in a structured environment.
evidence: This is a key observation comparing phenotypes on homogeneous vs. structured substrates.

claim: NM IIA contributes in guiding the cellular phenotype in the absence of external guiding cues.
source: This suggests that NM IIA contributes in guiding the cellular phenotype in the absence of external guiding cues.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that NM IIA-KO phenotypes are more pronounced on homogeneous substrates.

claim: The loss of NM IIA reduces both surface tension and line tension.
source: Although we cannot distinguish the absolute values of NM IIA or NM IIB that contribute to σ or λ, our results show that the loss of NM IIA reduces both values, while the loss of NM IIB leads to an increase of both types of tension.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined observations of AFM measurements and micropattern experiments.

claim: The loss of NM IIB leads to an increase of both surface tension and line tension.
source: Although we cannot distinguish the absolute values of NM IIA or NM IIB that contribute to σ or λ, our results show that the loss of NM IIA reduces both values, while the loss of NM IIB leads to an increase of both types of tension.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined observations of AFM measurements and micropattern experiments.

claim: NM IIA-KO cells still possess NM IIB-derived elastic stability but lack dynamic tension leading to low intracellular forces.
source: NM IIA-KO cells still possess NM IIB-derived elastic stability but lack dynamic tension leading to low intracellular forces.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Without NM IIA motors, NM IIB is too slow to rearrange the contractile forces in accordance with the fast polymerization of actin filaments at FAs.
source: Without NM IIA motors, NM IIB is too slow to rearrange the contractile forces in accordance with the fast polymerization of actin filaments at FAs.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the known motor properties and experimental observations.

claim: The generation of contractile actomyosin bundles is a mechanosensitive process.
source: Since the generation of contractile actomyosin bundles is a mechanosensitive process (Tojkander et al., 2015), a polarized actomyosin cytoskeleton is missing in NM IIA-KO cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research on mechanosensitivity.

claim: The only remaining stress fibers in NM IIA-KO cells resemble ventral stress fibers because their turnover is lowest.
source: The only remaining SF resemble ventral SF, because their turnover is lowest (Kumar et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is explained by citations to studies on stress fiber turnover rates.

claim: NM IIB-KO cells still possess NM IIA minifilaments, which generate sufficient but unbalanced intracellular forces.
source: NM IIB-KO cells in contrast still possess NM IIA minifilaments, which generate sufficient but unbalanced intracellular forces.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental observations on NM IIB-KO cells.

claim: The fast and dynamic motor activity of NM IIA is sufficient to induce the mechanosensitive assembly of all SF subtypes.
source: Although the fast and dynamic motor activity of NM IIA is sufficient to induce the mechanosensitive assembly of all SF subtypes, their distinct localization is disturbed (Shutova et al., 2017; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2008).
evidence: This is concluded from observations on NM IIB-KO cells and supported by citations.

claim: Loss of NM IIB does not affect the formation of FAs, however, they do not grow to full size.
source: Likewise, loss of NM IIB does not affect the formation of FAs, however, they do not grow to full size, since the actin templates are not sufficiently stabilized by the cross-linking properties of NM IIB (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2011).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data and explained by a citation to previous research.

claim: No phenotypic change or disturbance in the R(d) correlation was observed when depleting NM IIC.
source: No phenotypic change or disturbance in the R(d) correlation was observed when depleting NM IIC.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the micropattern experiments.

claim: NM IIC might be less important for the morphodynamics of single cells, at least in the U2OS cell line.
source: Thus, our results indicate that NM IIC might be less important for the morphodynamics of single cells, at least in our cell line.
evidence: This is concluded from the lack of phenotypic changes in NM IIC-KO cells on micropatterns.

claim: The model focuses on the crossbridge cycle properties in the motor heads and is sufficient to explain the experimentally observed R(d) relations on the micropattern.
source: Our model focuses on the crossbridge cycle properties in the motor heads and is sufficient to explain the experimentally observed R(d) relations on the micropattern.
evidence: This describes the scope and success of the mathematical model.

claim: The NM II isoforms differ in their tail regions, leading to marked differences in minifilament assembly/disassembly dynamics and intracellular localization patterns.
source: It is important to note that in addition, the NM II isoforms differ in their tail regions, leading to marked differences in minifilament assembly/disassembly dynamics and intracellular localization patterns (Breckenridge et al., 2009; Juanes-Garcia et al., 2015; Kaufmann and Schwarz, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on myosin tail regions.

claim: NM IIA-KO cells did not respond at all to the stretch-release cycle.
source: As expected, NM IIA-KO cells did not respond at all to the stretch-release cycle (Hippler et al., 2020).
evidence: This is observed in the stretch-release experiments and supported by a citation.

claim: A clear response was observed when stretching NM IIB-KO cells, however, the force increase did not reach the values of WT cells.
source: A clear response was observed when stretching NM IIB-KO cells, however, the force increase did not reach the values of WT cells.
evidence: This is observed in the stretch-release experiments.

claim: After releasing the stretch, cellular contraction forces in NM IIB-KO cells decreased to the initial level, but force decrease was accompanied with oscillations of contractile pulses in about 50% of analyzed traces.
source: After releasing the stretch, cellular contraction forces also decreased to the initial level, however, force decrease was accompanied with oscillations of contractile pulses in about 50% of analyzed traces (Figure 5—animation 7 and red trace in Figure 5—figure supplement 2) as compared to 10% in WT cells.
evidence: This is observed in the stretch-release experiments and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: NM IIB seems to regulate the spatiotemporal response of the actomyosin system by stabilizing NM IIA induced tension.
source: Thus, we again conclude that NM IIB seems to regulate the spatiotemporal response of the actomyosin system by stabilizing NM IIA induced tension.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the stretch-release experiments showing oscillations in NM IIB-KO cells.

claim: NM IIB-KO cells contracted collagen gels to a lower amount than WT cells.
source: We observed the same trend in collagen gels, where NM IIB-KO cells did contract the gel to a lower amount than WT cells, which is in good agreement with results of others (Meshel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is observed in the collagen gel experiments and supported by a citation.

claim: In about 80% of the analyzed NM IIC-KO cells, contraction forces did not relax to the initial setpoint within the observed timeframe of 30 min.
source: In about 80% of the analyzed NM IIC-KO cells, contraction forces did not relax to the initial setpoint within the observed timeframe of 30 min, while this was only the case for 20% of the WT cells.
evidence: This is quantified from the stretch-release experiments.

claim: NM IIC minifilaments are smaller compared to their paralog counterparts.
source: Structural in vitro analysis revealed that NM IIC minifilaments are smaller compared to their paralog counterparts (Billington et al., 2013).
evidence: This structural information is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: NM IIA and NM IIC co-localize throughout the whole cell body in U2OS cells.
source: As it was reported that NM IIA and NM IIC co-localize throughout the whole cell body in U2OS cells (Beach et al., 2014), this could suggest that NM IIC has a role as a scaffolding protein during the formation of higher ordered NM IIA minifilament stacks (Fenix et al., 2016), comparable to the role of myosin-18B (Jiu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on localization and potential scaffolding roles.

claim: NM IIC was shown to regulate the geometry of the epithelial apical junctional-line.
source: In epithelial sheets, NM IIC was shown to regulate the geometry of the epithelial apical junctional-line (Ebrahim et al., 2013) and the microvilli length (Chinowsky et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on epithelial cells.

claim: The phenotypic switch during EMT and the subsequent invasiveness of murine mammary gland cells goes along with a downregulation of NM IIC and an upregulation of NM IIB.
source: Strikingly, Beach and colleagues showed that the phenotypic switch during EMT (epithelial-mesenchymal transition) and the subsequent invasiveness of murine mammary gland cells goes along with a downregulation of NM IIC and an upregulation of NM IIB (Beach et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on EMT.

claim: The initiation of environmental guidance of the actomyosin system depends on the presence of NM IIA.
source: In summary, we showed that the environmental guidance of the actomyosin system follows a logical order. The initiation depends on the presence of NM IIA.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from all the experimental and modeling results.

claim: NM IIA can quickly repopulate newly formed protrusions and initiate new contraction sites.
source: This motor can quickly repopulate newly formed protrusions and initiate new contraction sites (Baird et al., 2017), giving rise to heterotypic minifilaments and dynamizing NM IIB (Fenix et al., 2016; Shutova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on NM IIA dynamics.

claim: Once the contraction is initiated, NM IIB co-assembles into the preformed contraction site and stabilizes the tension.
source: Once the contraction is initiated, NM IIB co-assembles into the preformed contraction site and stabilizes the tension, as this motor is prone to maintain tension on longer timescales by staying longer bound to the actin cytoskeleton (Sandquist and Means, 2008; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on NM IIB function.

claim: The stability of the heterotypic minifilaments is facilitated by the relative composition of NM IIA and NM IIB.
source: Thus, the stability of the heterotypic minifilaments is facilitated by the relative composition of NM IIA and NM IIB (Kaufmann and Schwarz, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a theoretical study.

claim: NM IIC might contribute to the actomyosin system as a structural regulator that controls force maintenance and relaxation, especially in a dynamical context.
source: NM IIC might contribute to this set-up as a structural regulator that controls force maintenance and relaxation, especially in a dynamical context, when external conditions change and homeostasis has to be ensured.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the observed role of NM IIC in force relaxation.
